details: Rankine cycle for nuclear power generation: thermodynamic cycle: water → heat → steam → turbine → condenser → pump → back to reactor; RBMK-1000 parameters: thermal power: 3200 MWt (100% rated); electrical output: 1000 MWe (gross); net electrical: ~925 MWe (station services subtracted); thermal efficiency η = W_electric / Q_thermal = 1000/3200 = 31.25%; Carnot efficiency limit: η_Carnot = 1 - T_cold/T_hot = 1 - (293K)/(560K) = 47.7% (theoretical max for RBMK conditions); gap from Carnot to actual: losses in: turbine isentropic efficiency (~85-88%); condenser heat rejection; pump work; heat exchanger losses; comparison: modern PWR (300°C steam): η = 33-36%; modern coal plant: 38-45%; gas turbine combined cycle: 55-60%; nuclear plants intrinsically lower efficiency than fossil fuel plants due to lower steam temperature (nuclear safety limits T and P of primary circuit)
chernobyl_application: RBMK turbine parameters: steam pressure at HP turbine inlet: 6.3 MPa (63 bar); steam temperature: 284°C (saturation; wet steam); turbine type: 2× K-500-65/3000 turbines per unit (each 500 MWe); steam flow rate: 5600 t/hr to turbines; LP turbine exhaust to condenser: 3.4 kPa (0.034 bar); condenser cooling: Pripyat River water (once-through) or cooling pond (22.9 km²); turbine house: 200m long; turbine hall = building where safety test was conducted April 25-26 1986 (test: how long turbine coast-down maintains cooling pumps after steam cutoff); test required low power (700-1000 MWt) → xenon pit → accident
source: Knief 1992; El-Wakil 1971 Nuclear Heat Transport; rbmk_thermal_hydraulics_REAL.csv

details: Power density and heat flux in RBMK: average volumetric power density: 5 W/cm³ (core volume ~5000 m³; total thermal power 3200 MW); peak power density (hot spot): ~15 W/cm³ at fuel centerline of highest-power channel; fuel centerline temperature (nominal full power): ~900-1100°C (UO₂ melting point: 2865°C; fuel operating at 300-400°C below melt); cladding surface temperature: 325-340°C (subcooled boiling); heat flux at cladding: q'' = kUO₂ × (T_center - T_surface) / (r²/4) = ~0.5-1.5 MW/m²; critical Heat Flux (CHF) = departure from nucleate boiling (DNB): q''_CHF for RBMK at 7 MPa ≈ 2-4 MW/m²; safety margin: q''/q''_CHF = 0.3-0.8 (normal operation); RBMK April 26 during excursion: q'' reached 200-400× normal in 4 seconds → q''/q''_CHF >> 1 → film boiling → cladding failure → fuel dispersal
chernobyl_application: RBMK vs PWR power density comparison: PWR average ~100 W/cm³ (10m³ core for 3000 MWt); RBMK 5 W/cm³ (660m³ core for 3200 MWt); PWR factor 20× more compact; PWR advantages: smaller pressure vessel; higher efficiency per volume; RBMK advantage: individual channel = local failure contained (in principle); PWR pressure vessel failure = entire primary circuit fails; but RBMK size = larger building + positive void coefficient; power density calculation: Unit 4 at 200 MW (0.8% power night of April 26): average 5 × 0.008 = 0.04 W/cm³; excursion peak: 200 W/cm³ momentarily (200× rated power in highest channels) → CHF exceeded by factor 50-100 → catastrophic failure

details: Decay heat physics: after shutdown (scram), fission stops but beta/gamma decay of fission products continues; ANS-5.1 (1979) standard formula: P(t) = 0.066 × P₀ × [t⁻⁰·² - (t+t₀)⁻⁰·²] where P₀ = steady-state power; t = time after shutdown (seconds); t₀ = operating time; approximate: at 1 second: P/P₀ ≈ 7%; at 1 minute: P/P₀ ≈ 3.3%; at 1 hour: P/P₀ ≈ 1.5%; at 1 day: P/P₀ ≈ 0.6%; at 1 year: P/P₀ ≈ 0.1%; for RBMK-1000 at 3200 MWt rated: at 1 minute after shutdown: decay heat = 3200 × 0.033 = 106 MW; at 1 day: 3200 × 0.006 = 19.2 MW; cooling requirement: must continue cooling for days after shutdown to prevent fuel damage; LOCA (loss of coolant accident): if cooling stops, decay heat alone can melt fuel within minutes
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl April 26: ECCS (Emergency Core Cooling System) was deliberately disabled before test (safety test requirement to test turbine coast-down without ECCS actuation); at moment of accident: reactor at 200 MWt (0.8% power) → went prompt critical → 30,000 MWt in <4s → fuel exploded; decay heat from 200 MWt operation was irrelevant compared to excursion; BUT: after explosion: core scattered; decay heat from scattered fuel particles = ongoing heat source; graphite fire sustained by decay heat + combustion; corium formation: residual fuel (in basement, under reactor) heated by decay heat → melted → solidified; modern RBMK and all new reactor designs: decay heat removal = primary passive safety requirement; Gen IV passive safety concepts: natural convection decay heat removal without pumps
source: ANS-5.1 1979; Todreas Kazimi 1990 Nuclear Systems Vol I; rbmk_thermal_hydraulics_REAL.csv; chernobyl_spent_fuel_isf2_REAL.csv

details: Boiling heat transfer regimes in RBMK channels: (1) Single-phase convection (subcooled region near channel inlet): q'' = h × (T_wall - T_bulk); h = 30,000-50,000 W/(m²·K) for turbulent flow; (2) Nucleate boiling (normal operating mode in upper channel): q'' = h × (T_wall - T_sat)ⁿ; h greatly enhanced (500,000-1,000,000 W/(m²·K) effective); high heat flux with small temperature difference; (3) Critical heat flux (CHF): transition from nucleate to film boiling; heat transfer coefficient drops 100-1000×; cladding temperature spike → fuel damage; (4) Film boiling (post-CHF): vapor film insulates cladding; cladding temperature rises rapidly; Zircaloy-water reaction begins >900°C; (5) DNB (Departure from Nucleate Boiling): in PWR; occurs at high flux; (6) Dryout: in BWR/RBMK; steam quality exceeds threshold; dry patch → film boiling
chernobyl_application: RBMK normal operating regime: each channel at ~19% steam quality; designed to avoid CHF with safety margin; flow: 17-28 kg/s per channel depending on power; at accident conditions: channels near Unit 4 explosion received: (1) Instantaneous power increase 200× rated → heat flux 200× → immediate CHF exceeded → film boiling → Zr oxidation; (2) Loss of coolant (steam explosion destroyed pressure circuit) → dry out → cladding failure; two simultaneous heat transfer failure modes; heat transfer coefficient during accident = 0 (steam blanket + dry out); time to cladding failure: <1 second; time to fuel dispersal: 3-4 seconds (explosion timescale); consistent with chronology: power excursion 01:23:40-44 → explosion 01:23:44
source: Collier 1972 Convective Boiling and Condensation; Tong 1979 Nuclear Heat Transfer; rbmk_thermal_hydraulics_REAL.csv

details: Chernobyl explosion mechanism debate: TWO explosions confirmed (witnesses; seismic records; destruction pattern): FIRST explosion (01:23:44): current scientific consensus (Kholosha 1997; INSAG-7; Schentler 2001): prompt criticality power excursion → superheat of coolant to 500-1000°C → explosive flashing of water to steam (steam explosion) → destructive overpressure ~10 MPa → lifted reactor lid (~200 tonnes) off reactor vessel → breached building roof; evidence: blue flash/light observed (Cherenkov radiation from intense fission); seismic station recorded ~3.0 MW(s) at 01:23:44; SECOND explosion (01:23:47; ~3 seconds later): hydrogen detonation; H₂ from Zr-water reaction (massive H₂ production in 3s between explosions) + H₂ from water radiolysis → mixed with air entering through first explosion breach → detonation; evidence: red-orange fireball (hydrocarbon combustion + hydrogen); larger overpressure damage; roof and wall destruction
chernobyl_application: Alternative hypotheses: (1) Pure steam explosion (both): proponents argue H₂ insufficient in 3 seconds; (2) Nuclear detonation: rejected by all experts (impossible in LWR geometry; supercriticality cannot sustain in LWR; Chernobyl = thermal criticality excursion not nuclear weapon explosion); (3) INSAG-1 (original 1986): blamed operators; INSAG-7 (1992): added design fault as co-equal cause; (4) Steinberg 2008 controversial paper: argued second explosion was nuclear; consensus rejection: geometry, neutron physics prevent nuclear detonation in reactor fuel; distinction matters: steam explosion causes LOCa; H₂ detonation causes building destruction; both occurred; Chernobyl destruction pattern consistent with combination; seismic evidence supports at least one large mechanical explosion + one chemical/H₂ detonation
source: INSAG-7 1992; Kholosha 1997 J Nucl Energy; chernobyl_accident_chronology_REAL.csv; rbmk_thermal_hydraulics_REAL.csv; reactor_coolant_chemistry_REAL.csv

details: Density Wave Oscillations (DWO) in RBMK: two-phase flow instability; mechanism: pressure drop across channel oscillates at natural frequency → flow oscillates → steam void fraction oscillates → power oscillates (via positive void coefficient) → feed-forward instability; frequency: 0.1-1 Hz (natural period 1-10 seconds); Ledinegg instability: static flow instability (multiple steady-state operating points on pressure-flow curve); RBMK susceptibility: individual channels → each channel can independently undergo DWO; at low power + low flow (April 26 test conditions at 200 MWt): DWO most likely; operators observed: erratic power fluctuations before AZ-5 press → consistent with DWO in multiple channels; DWO + positive void coefficient = amplifying feedback; DWO first analyzed for RBMK in classified 1983 VNIIAES report; recommendations not implemented; disclosed publicly only in 1991
chernobyl_application: DWO contribution to Chernobyl: at 200 MWt with many channels near boiling onset: DWO likely occurring in multiple channels simultaneously; power fluctuations observed by Toptunov before final excursion → consistent with DWO; Leonenko et al. 1989 (Soviet publication): reconstructed pre-accident power history shows periodic oscillations at 0.2 Hz = DWO signature; in absence of AZ-5 press: DWO could have been operator-managed by inserting rods manually; AZ-5 press attempted to shut down reactor experiencing DWO + high power trend → graphite tip effect reversed the shutdown → prompt criticality; interaction: DWO (destabilizing) + graphite tip (destabilizing) + positive void coefficient (destabilizing) + ORM=8 (insufficient margin) = perfect instability scenario
source: Leonenko 1989 Soviet Physics; rbmk_thermal_hydraulics_REAL.csv; rbmk_void_coefficient_physics_REAL.csv; rbmk_core_neutron_physics_REAL.csv

details: Chernobyl cooling pond thermal hydraulics: area: 22.9 km²; volume: 151 million m³; purpose: reject condenser heat (Units 1-4); design heat rejection: 4 × 2200 MWt rejected to pond = 8800 MWt maximum; retention time: 1.5-2 years; evaporation: ~50% of heat rejection via evaporation; sensible heat to water: ~50%; temperature rise: ΔT = Q / (ρ × V × cp) per year = 8800 MWt × 3.15×10⁷ s/yr / (1000 kg/m³ × 1.51×10⁸ m³ × 4186 J/kg/K) = 0.44°C/yr (steady state: heat in = heat out); steady state pond temperature: ~20-25°C (summer) = above river temperature by 3-5°C; biological effects: warm water → enhanced biological productivity → catfish; carp; large predatory fish; post-1986: no active heat rejection (reactors shut down); pond slowly cooling to ambient; 2014 drawdown: engineered drainage to allow land area access for ISF-2 construction; Sr-90 remobilization event
chernobyl_application: Thermal ecology of cooling pond: elevated temperature → thermal plume → enhanced algal growth → nutrient cycling → higher fish productivity; catfish (Silurus glanis) in pond: up to 96,000 Bq/kg Cs-137 (cez_wildlife_contamination_REAL.csv); WHY big fish: long-lived; predatory (bioaccumulation); warm water pond (growth-favorable); post-drawdown 2014: Sr-90 in sediment porewater exposed to oxygen → oxidizing conditions → Sr-90 mobilized → peak Sr-90 in Pripyat floodplain groundwater 102 kBq/m³ (10× WHO guideline); thermal ecology effects on radionuclide cycling: biological pump in pond → Cs-137 in zooplankton → fish; thermal stratification → vertical mixing → sediment interaction

details: UO₂ fuel thermal properties: thermal conductivity: k = 3.6 W/(m·K) at 900°C (decreases with temperature and burnup); Wiedemann-Franz law does not apply (ceramic; ionic conductor); radial temperature profile in cylindrical fuel: T(r) = T_surface + q'''/(4k) × (R²-r²); for q''' = 150 W/cm³ (RBMK); R = 4.65mm (fuel pellet radius): ΔT_fuel = q'''R²/4k = 1.5×10⁸ × (4.65×10⁻³)² / (4 × 4) = 202°C; T_centerline = T_surface + 202°C = 340 + 202 = 542°C (at rated power); actual: higher due to lower k at temperature; burnup effect: fission gas (Xe, Kr) in fuel matrix → thermal conductivity degradation; at high burnup: k can drop to 2-2.5 W/m/K; centerline temperature: 800-1100°C at rated power; UO₂ melting point: 2865°C; design margin: at least 1700°C below melt
chernobyl_application: UO₂ at accident conditions: during excursion 200× power: q''' = 200 × 150 = 30,000 W/cm³; ΔT_fuel = 30,000 × (4.65×10⁻³)² × 10⁸ / (4 × 4) = 40,000°C calculated → physical limit: UO₂ melts at 2865°C; fuel completely melts within 0.1 seconds; molten UO₂ (density 9,300 kg/m³; liquid) → fuel dispersal by steam pressure; UO₂ vaporization point: 3242°C; at 200× power: UO₂ vapor pressure significant → explosive phase change → fuel fragments propelled at high velocity; solid → liquid → vapor transition all occurred in <1 second during excursion; explains fuel particle size distribution: from 4 µm (condensed vapor) to 150 µm (solidified droplets) to cm-scale (fragmented pellets)
source: Olander 1976 Fundamental Aspects of Nuclear Reactor Fuel Elements; rbmk_fuel_specifications_REAL.csv; fuel_particle_contamination_REAL.csv; atmospheric_aerosol_physics_REAL.csv
